+  "summary": "Neko: Authorization bypass in legacy WebRTC input handling",
+  "details": "### Impact\n\nWhen legacy mode is enabled and `session.implicit_hosting` is enabled, the legacy WebRTC data channel incorrectly authorizes input events due to a logic error in `LegacyIsHost()`.\n\nAs a result, an authenticated room member may be able to send mouse and keyboard input through the legacy WebRTC control channel even when controls are locked or the member would otherwise not be authorized through the modern control API.\n\nThe issue affects only the legacy WebRTC input path. The modern HTTP/WebSocket control path correctly enforces authorization checks and is not affected.\n\nTo exploit this issue, an attacker must:\n\n* Be authenticated as a room member.\n* Successfully establish a WebRTC connection.\n* Access a deployment using the legacy WebRTC input handler.\n\nNo unauthenticated access or privilege escalation outside the application is possible.\n\n### Patches\n\nThe issue has been fixed in **[v3.1.5](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko/releases/tag/v3.1.5)** by correcting the authorization logic in the legacy WebRTC handler.\n\nUsers should upgrade to **[v3.1.5](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko/releases/tag/v3.1.5)** or later. Fix: *[395ca1a](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko/commit/395ca1a6f62b7b0e270e654d366a2d57b8042efd)*\n\n### Workarounds\n\nUsers who cannot immediately upgrade can mitigate the issue by one of the following:\n\n* Disable legacy mode if it is not required.\n* Disable implicit hosting (`session.implicit_hosting=false`).\n* Restrict access to trusted authenticated users.\n\n### Credits\n\nThanks to @KasperBuilds for responsibly disclosing this vulnerability and reaching out directly. This contribution helped strengthen the project, and the whole community benefits from it.",

+{
+  "schema_version": "1.4.0",
+  "id": "GHSA-5h93-6whr-6q8j",
+  "modified": "2026-10-27T21:05:35Z",
+  "published": "2026-10-27T21:05:34Z",
+  "aliases": [
+    "CVE-2026-116685"
+  ],
+  "summary": "Model Context Protocol Python SDK: HTTP client transports followed cross-origin redirects carrying custom headers and bodies",
+  "details": "### Summary\nIn affected versions, the SDK's Streamable HTTP and SSE client transports followed HTTP redirects to any host. If the configured MCP endpoint answered with a redirect to a different origin:\n\n- custom headers set on the client (for example an `X-API-Key` credential) were sent to that origin, and\n- on a `307` or `308` redirect the request body was re-sent there too.\n\nThe SDK's OAuth client providers followed redirects on their own discovery, registration and token requests in the same way.\n\nA lone `Authorization` bearer header was not exposed; the HTTP library already drops it on cross-origin redirects.\n\nAnyone able to make an endpoint you trust redirect elsewhere (a stale redirect to a lapsed domain, a misrouted proxy rule, redirect logic an attacker can influence) could capture that material. A server that is itself malicious gains nothing this way; it already receives your requests directly.\n\n### Am I affected?\nYes, if your code uses the SDK as an MCP client over HTTP through any of:\n\n- `streamable_http_client` (on 2.x also `Client` given an `http://` or `https://` URL)\n- `streamablehttp_client` or `sse_client`\n- `ClientSessionGroup` with HTTP server parameters\n- the internal `create_mcp_http_client` helper\n\nThis includes an HTTP client you passed in yourself with `follow_redirects=True`.\n\nAffected versions: 1.8.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.\n\nNot affected:\n\n- MCP servers\n- stdio clients\n- a client you supplied with `follow_redirects` left at its default of `False`\n\n### Fix\nUpgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later; no code changes are needed.\n\nThe transports, and the OAuth providers' own requests, now follow a redirect only when it stays on the endpoint's origin (same scheme, host and port, or an `http` to `https` upgrade on the same host) and keeps the request method. Any other redirect is not followed and the request fails with an error naming the target (`MCPError` on 2.x, `httpx.HTTPStatusError` on 1.x), whichever HTTP client the transport uses. The internal `create_mcp_http_client` helper no longer turns redirect following on, so code calling it directly now receives the redirect response instead.\n\nIf your client currently reaches its server through a redirect to another host, including a server that needs no credentials, it will stop connecting after the upgrade: set the endpoint URL to the redirect's target.\n\nUntil you can upgrade, supply your own HTTP client with `follow_redirects` left at `False` (`http_client=` on `streamable_http_client`; `httpx_client_factory=` on `sse_client` and `streamablehttp_client`; `ClientSessionGroup` has no such parameter). If a client may already have followed a redirect to a host you do not control, rotate the credentials it carried.\n\n<details>\n<summary>If you genuinely need the old behaviour (unsupported)</summary>\n\nThis restores what this advisory fixes: redirects to any host are followed again, carrying your custom headers and, on `307`/`308`, the request body, OAuth token requests included. Prefer setting the endpoint URL to the redirect's target. If you cannot, and you accept forwarding credentials to the redirect target, give the transport an HTTP client that follows redirects regardless of what the SDK asks for:\n\n```python\nimport httpx2  # on 1.x: import httpx and subclass httpx.AsyncClient instead\n\nclass FollowRedirectsAnyway(httpx2.AsyncClient):\n    \"\"\"Follows redirects to ANY origin. Deliberately gives up the SDK's same-origin protection.\"\"\"\n\n    async def send(self, request, *, follow_redirects=False, **kwargs):\n        return await super().send(request, follow_redirects=True, **kwargs)\n\nhttp_client = FollowRedirectsAnyway(timeout=httpx2.Timeout(30, read=300))\n# streamable_http_client(url, http_client=http_client)\n\n# sse_client / streamablehttp_client take a factory instead:\ndef client_factory(headers=None, timeout=None, auth=None):\n    return FollowRedirectsAnyway(headers=headers, auth=auth,\n                                 timeout=timeout if timeout is not None else httpx2.Timeout(30, read=300))\n# sse_client(url, httpx_client_factory=client_factory)\n```\n\nThe redirect handling is then the HTTP library's own, as before the fix: a lone `Authorization` header is still dropped on cross-origin hops and `301`/`302`/`303` become `GET`. It is not something the SDK supports or tests.\n\n</details>\n\n---",

+  "summary": "OpenTelemetry Python: Unbounded memory allocation in Jaeger baggage propagation",
+  "details": "## Summary\n\n`JaegerPropagator.extract()` in `opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger` did not enforce limits when extracting inbound `uberctx-*` baggage headers. Attacker-controlled baggage could cause unnecessary CPU work and short-lived heap allocations while processing more data than the propagator should accept.\n\n## Impact\n\nServices that enable the optional Jaeger propagator and accept untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request resource usage. This can contribute to denial-of-service risk when transport-level limits are absent or configured above the baggage limits.\n\nThe practical impact for most Python web deployments is limited. The package must be installed separately, and the Jaeger propagator is not enabled by the default OpenTelemetry Python configuration.\n\nCommon Python web servers also constrain request headers before they reach the propagator:\n\n- Gunicorn allows a maximum of 100 request-header fields and 8,190 bytes per field by default.\n- Uvicorn’s h11 implementation limits its incomplete-event buffer to 16,384 bytes by default.\n\nThe risk is higher for non-HTTP transports, custom `TextMapGetter` implementations, or deployments where server and gateway limits have been increased or disabled.\n\nThe impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.\n\n## Patches\n\nVersions of `opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger` earlier than `1.45.0` are affected.\n\nUpgrade `opentelemetry-propagator-jaeger` to version `1.45.0` or later.\n\nVersion `1.45.0` limits extraction to 180 entries and 8,192 total bytes and skips entries larger than 4,096 bytes.\n\n## Credit\n\ntonghuaroot",

@@ -0,0 +1,80 @@
+{
+  "schema_version": "1.4.0",
+  "id": "GHSA-rjh2-4xgw-p2hj",
+  "modified": "2026-10-27T21:04:50Z",
+  "published": "2026-10-27T21:04:50Z",
+  "aliases": [
+    "CVE-2026-116676"
+  ],
+  "summary": "Atlantis: OS command injection through PR-controlled Terraform workspace enables RCE during plan",
+  "details": "### Summary

Atlantis passes the Terraform `workspace` value from a pull request's `atlantis.yaml` into a shell command without quoting or escaping it.

A contributor whose pull request is eligible for an Atlantis plan can include shell metacharacters in the workspace name and execute arbitrary commands as the Atlantis service account. This does not require custom workflows, `allow_custom_workflows`, or permission to run `terraform apply`.

The executed command inherits the Atlantis process environment, which commonly contains cloud-provider, Terraform, and VCS credentials.

### Details

Verified against current `upstream/main` commit `92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984` on August 13, 2026.

The vulnerable data flow is:

1. The PR-controlled project workspace is validated in [`server/core/config/raw/project.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/config/raw/project.go#L139-L149).

   Validation rejects only `..`, `/`, and `\`. Shell metacharacters such as `;`, `#`, `$`, redirections, and whitespace remain permitted.

2. The workspace is passed directly as a Terraform command argument in [`server/core/runtime/workspace_step_runner_delegate.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/runtime/workspace_step_runner_delegate.go#L86-L96):

   ```go
   []string{workspaceCmd, "select", ctx.Workspace}
   ```

3. Terraform arguments are concatenated into a single string using `strings.Join(args, " ")` in [`server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go#L451-L468):

   ```go
   tfCmd := fmt.Sprintf("%s %s", binPath, strings.Join(args, " "))
   ```

4. The resulting string is executed through `sh -c` in [`server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go`](https://github.com/runatlantis/atlantis/blob/92ce5c51d1a050357e44df3535483425e59fa984/server/core/terraform/tfclient/terraform_client.go#L416-L427):

   ```go
   cmd := exec.Command("sh", "-c", tfCmd)
   ```

Consequently, a workspace such as:

```text
poc;id;false;#
```

produces commands equivalent to:

```sh
terraform workspace select poc;id;false;#
terraform workspace new poc;id;false;#
```

`raw.Project.Validate()` was confirmed to return no error for this workspace value.

Atlantis documents that planning untrusted Terraform can already be dangerous because providers and external data sources execute code. The distinct issue here is that an ordinary project configuration field becomes shell source, bypassing the explicit `allow_custom_workflows` control and requiring no malicious provider, external data source, custom workflow, or apply operation.

The primary remediation should be to execute Terraform using an argument vector rather than constructing shell source—for example, `exec.Command(binaryPath, args...)`. Any required environment-variable expansion should be performed without invoking a shell. Strict workspace-name validation would also provide defense in depth.

### PoC

Only reproduce this against a disposable Atlantis instance and test repository.

#### Preconditions

- Atlantis processes `atlantis.yaml` from the pull request branch.
- The pull request is eligible to run `atlantis plan`.
- For a fork pull request, the server must have `--allow-fork-prs` enabled. A same-repository branch does not require this flag.
- No custom workflows or apply permissions are required.

#### Repository contents

Create `main.tf`:

```hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.0"
}
```

Create `atlantis.yaml`:

```yaml
version: 3
projects:
  - name: workspace-rce-poc
    dir: .
    workspace: "poc;id;false;#"
    autoplan:
      enabled: false
```

Open a pull request containing these files and comment:

```text
atlantis plan -p workspace-rce-poc
```

#### Expected result

Atlantis first runs `terraform workspace select`. The injected `false` causes that command invocation to return an error, so Atlantis retries using `terraform workspace new`.

On both attempts, the shell executes `id` as a separate command. The second failure includes the combined command output in the Atlantis error response, exposing output similar to:

```text
uid=1000(atlantis) gid=1000(atlantis) groups=1000(atlantis)
```

This demonstrates arbitrary shell-command execution without creating a custom workflow or reaching the apply phase.

The payload uses only `id` and `false` and does not access credentials, make network requests, or modify the host beyond Terraform potentially creating the disposable `poc` workspace.

### Impact

This is an OS command injection vulnerability  resulting in remote code execution as the Atlantis service account.

Affected deployments are those that:

- Process pull-request-controlled `atlantis.yaml` project configuration; and
- Permit the attacker-controlled pull request to trigger an Atlantis plan.

Potential consequences include:

- Reading and exfiltrating cloud-provider, Terraform, and VCS credentials inherited from the Atlantis process.
- Accessing Terraform state, plan files, repository checkouts, caches, and other data available to the Atlantis user.
- Modifying files or binaries accessible to the service account.
- Making network requests using the Atlantis server's network identity.
- Pivoting into infrastructure accessible through the server's credentials or network placement.

For public repositories, arbitrary external contributors are directly exposed when `--allow-fork-prs` is enabled. Without fork PR support, the vulnerable population includes users able to create eligible same-repository pull requests and attackers controlling such accounts.",

+  "summary": "Model Context Protocol Python SDK: Client fetched server-chosen $ref URLs while validating tool results against output schemas",
+  "details": "### Summary\nIn affected versions, when a connected MCP server declared an `outputSchema` for a tool, the SDK's client validated each `call_tool` result with `jsonschema`'s default resolver, which fetches any `$ref` it cannot resolve locally by opening the URL. A server could therefore put an `http://`, `https://` or `file://` reference in a tool's output schema and make the client:\n\n- request that URL, or read that local file, from the client's own network position on every call of the tool (the content was used only as a schema and never sent back to the server), and\n- stall: the fetch ran synchronously on the event loop with no timeout, so a target that accepted the connection and then went quiet froze every session in the process for as long as it held the connection.\n\n### Am I affected?\nYes, if your application uses the SDK as an MCP client (`ClientSession` over any transport, `ClientSessionGroup`, or the 2.x `Client`) and calls tools on servers you do not fully control. There was no setting that turned the validation off.\n\nAffected versions: 1.10.0 through 1.29.1, and 2.0.0 through 2.1.1.\n\nNot affected: applications that only build servers. If nothing in your code uses `ClientSession`, `ClientSessionGroup` or the 2.x `Client` class, you are not affected.\n\n### Fix\nUpgrade to `mcp` 1.30.0 (1.x) or 2.2.0 (2.x) or later. The client now resolves references only within the schema document the server sent (plus the standard JSON Schema metaschemas), so result validation performs no network or file access. A tool whose output schema points outside its own document fails at call time with `RuntimeError` (`Invalid schema for tool ...`); in-document references such as `#/$defs/...` work as before.\n\nUntil you can upgrade, call tools only on servers you trust. As a partial stopgap, skip tools whose `outputSchema` contains an `$id`, or a `$ref` / `$dynamicRef` that does not start with `#`.",

+  "summary": "Model Context Protocol Python SDK: Server bearer-token authentication accepts tokens issued for a different resource server",
+  "details": "### Summary\nIn affected versions, the SDK's server-side bearer authentication had no way to check that a token was issued for your server (its audience). Where one authorization server issues tokens for several services, a valid token for another service was also accepted by your MCP server.\n\n### Am I affected?\nYes, if your HTTP server uses the SDK's bearer authentication (`auth=AuthSettings(...)` with `token_verifier=`), its authorization server also issues tokens for other services, and your `TokenVerifier` does not check the token's audience (`aud`) itself.\n\nAffected versions:\n\n- `mcp` 1.10.0 through 1.29.1\n- `mcp` 2.0.0 through 2.1.1\n\n### Fix\nUpgrade to:\n\n- 1.x: `mcp` 1.30.0 or later\n- 2.x: `mcp` 2.2.0 or later\n\n**Upgrading alone changes nothing.** The patched versions add a `validate_token_resource` setting that is off unless you set it. To turn the check on, make both of these changes together:\n\n1. Set `validate_token_resource=True` in `AuthSettings`, with `resource_server_url` set to the audience your authorization server puts in tokens for your server.\n2. Return the token's audience from `verify_token()` as `AccessToken.resource`.\n\nA token for another service then gets `401`. With only the first change, every request gets `401`.\n\nIf your `TokenVerifier` already checks the audience, set `validate_token_resource=False` to silence the deprecation warning. The setting will default to `True` in 3.0.\n\nIf you cannot upgrade yet, reject any token whose `aud` does not include your server inside `verify_token()`. That closes the issue on every version.",

+  "summary": "dd-trace: ReDOS in URL query string obfuscation",
+  "details": "### Summary\n\nA regular expression used to obfuscate URL query strings can consume excessive CPU when processing certain attacker-controlled input. This can stall request processing and cause denial of service in applications using affected HTTP tracing integrations.\n\n### Details\n\nThe default query-string obfuscation pattern can exhibit excessive backtracking. The pattern is applied synchronously when recording HTTP URL metadata, allowing query-string processing to occupy application resources for an extended period.\n\nAs a workaround, set DD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP to the fixed regex below, then restart the application.\n\n```\nDD_TRACE_OBFUSCATION_QUERY_STRING_REGEXP='(?:(?:\"|%22)?)(?:(?:old[-_]?|new[-_]?)?p(?:ass)?w(?:or)?d(?:1|2)?|pass(?:[-_]?phrase)?|secret|(?:api[-_]?|private[-_]?|public[-_]?|access[-_]?|secret[-_]?|app(?:lication)?[-_]?)key(?:[-_]?id)?|token|consumer[-_]?(?:id|key|secret)|sign(?:ed|ature)?|auth(?:entication|orization)?)(?:(?:\\s|%20)*(?:=|%3D)[^&]+|(?:\"|%22)(?:\\s|%20)*(?::|%3A)(?:\\s|%20)*(?:\"|%22)(?:%2[^2]|%[^2]|[^\"%])+(?:\"|%22))|(?:bearer(?:\\s|%20)+[a-z0-9._\\-]+|token(?::|%3A)[a-z0-9]{13}|gh[opsu]_[0-9a-zA-Z]{36}|(?:(?<![\\w-])|(?<=%[0-9a-f]{2}))ey[I-L][\\w-]+(?:=|%3D)*\\.ey[I-L][\\w-]+(?:=|%3D)*(?:\\.(?:[\\w.+/=-]|%3D|%2F|%2B)+)?|-{5}BEGIN(?:[a-z\\s]|%20)+PRIVATE(?:\\s|%20)KEY-{5}[^\\-]+-{5}END(?:[a-z\\s]|%20)+PRIVATE(?:\\s|%20)KEY(?:-{5})?(?:\\n|%0A)?|(?:ssh-(?:rsa|dss)|ecdsa-[a-z0-9]+-[a-z0-9]+)(?:\\s|%20|%09)+(?:[a-z0-9/.+]|%2F|%5C|%2B){100,}(?:=|%3D)*(?:(?:\\s|%20|%09)+[a-z0-9._-]+)?)'\n```\n\n### Proof of concept\n\nDetailed triggering inputs and reproduction steps are omitted from this advisory. The patched version includes regression coverage for the affected behavior.\n\n### Impact\n\nRegular expression denial of service (ReDoS) affecting applications that process attacker-controlled URL query strings through the vulnerable obfuscation pattern.
